author: TGEU
title: Hungary removes anti-LGBTI provisions, but trans people are still left out
content:
TGEU welcomes the decision of the Hungarian National Assembly on 13 October, 2026 to remove the anti-LGBTI content from the 2021 ‘child protection’ law. This is a necessary step to implement the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) judgment in 

Commission v Hungary

 (C-769/22).




In its April 2026 judgment, the CJEU found that the law, which stigmatised LGBTI people under the guise of child protection, breached EU law. It also rejected Hungary’s reliance on national identity to justify discriminatory measures. 




Why this matters for trans people




The ruling matters for trans people across the EU, because it confirms that Member States cannot use ‘child protection’ or national identity as an excuse for excluding trans and other LGBTI people from public life and the rights EU law guarantees them. The CJEU has already held in 

Mirin

 (C-4/23) that Member States must recognise a legal gender change obtained in another Member State, so the Commission has clear legal grounds to act. The CJEU has also held in 

Deldits

 (C-247/23) that a Hungarian refusal to rectify a trans refugee’s gender marker breaches the GDPR, which further strengthens the case for Commission action.

author: Aoife Doran
title: Ceuta: Spain must protect trans asylum seekers, not return them to danger
content:
More than two months after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, many remain in precarious conditions, with inadequate access to shelter, essential services and international protection. Among them are trans asylum applicants who have fled persecution, only to face further violence, insecurity and the threat of being returned to danger. Their situation is part of a wider humanitarian crisis affecting people on the move in Ceuta, all of whom deserve safety, dignity and access to protection.




We are deeply concerned by reports of physical assaults, harassment and mistreatment of people seeking protection in Ceuta. A 

report by Border Resistance

, a grassroots collective working at the border, documents at least seven alleged incidents of violence against LGBTI people between 21 August and 6 September. One trans woman described being assaulted by police officers after being expelled from a reception centre, stating, 

“We are trans, we cannot live on the street because we are attacked.”

 Another described fleeing Morocco after receiving death threats from her family. These testimonies expose the grave risks facing trans and other LGBTI people who seek protection in Ceuta, only to encounter further violence and insecurity. We also reject the racist and dehumanising portrayal of people arriving in Ceuta as an

author: TGEU
title: TGEU publishes Know Your Rights: How EU Directives Protect Trans People. Second Revised Version
content:
This guide provides a basic overview of EU directives in which trans people are protected from discrimination, including through the explicit inclusion of the grounds of ‘gender reassignment’, ‘gender identity’, or ‘gender expression’. As such, it helps trans people to better understand and claim their fundamental rights. It also helps legal professionals, equality bodies, and policymakers to understand their legal obligations to ensure equal protection. 










Get the guide










What are EU directives?




EU directives are a type of EU law that sets goals Member States must reach through their own legislation. However, EU directives do not prescribe how Member States should implement them. In other words, EU directives set a common minimum standard but leave Member States flexibility in how they achieve it.




All EU directives must be ‘transposed’, a process that incorporates an EU directive into national legislation. Once a directive is adopted, transposition begins, and the directive itself sets a deadline for completion.







Objective of the guide




Since TGEU published our first Know Your Rights guide in 2015, additional EU directives have been adopted and are entering into force. These newer directives, which extend protections for trans people across a broader range of areas, form the focus of this guide.

author: TGEU
title: Join our webinar:  Countering Anti-Trans Misinformation – Tools, Tactics and Lessons from Across Europe
content:
Anti-trans misinformation is increasingly shaping public debates about trans rights across Europe. How do these narratives emerge, how do they travel across borders and platforms, and how can we respond effectively?




Join TGEU and the European Fact-Checking Standards Network (EFCSN) for a practical exchange between trans and LGBT organisations and fact-checkers from across Europe.




The webinar will explore common anti-trans misinformation narratives and how they are amplified and adapted in different contexts. It will also examine how fact-checking can help identify, contextualise, and respond to misleading claims.




Speakers from fact-checking organisations and TGEU members will share insights from their national and organisational contexts. A joint exercise and discussion will follow, focusing on approaches that can be adapted to different advocacy and communications contexts.




The session is an opportunity to learn from each other, build connections between the fact-checking and trans advocacy communities, and exchange practical approaches for responding to anti-trans misinformation online.

author: TGEU
title: Türkiye’s crackdown on LGBTI rights – the impact on trans people in prison
content:
Since 12 September 2026, Turkish authorities have intensified a nationwide crackdown on LGBTI people, organisations and human rights defenders. At least 117 people have reportedly been detained, with at least 83 held in pre-trial detention. 




The operation, branded “My Family is Safe” has involved arrests, raids on homes and organisations, digital restrictions, and the use of ‘public-morality’ and ‘obscenity’ provisions under Turkish criminal law. 







The impact on trans people




Criminalisation, discriminatory policing and restrictive prison practices in Türkiye come together to heighten risks for trans people in detention. At least 27 of those placed in pre-trial detention are trans women, many of whom have been charged with ‘prostitution’ and/or ‘obscenity’ offences. 




Trans detainees report strip searches and humiliating treatment and placement in detention arrangements that do not match their gender identity. Prison reports describe prolonged isolation, barriers to hormone treatment and HIV medication, limits on clothing and belongings, access to drinking water, overcrowding, and difficulty reaching legal and medical support.

author: Béla
title: Join our next PeerNetz session: building peer-led trans healthcare
content:
As part of our Peer Networking Zone (PeerNetz), TGEU is hosting a meeting to explore healthcare designed by and for trans people, rooted in community knowledge and care. We’ll be joined by Trans Healthcare Action, the organisation behind Kindred, Ireland’s first peer-led trans health clinic.




The session will be interactive, with practical exercises and space to explore how Kindred’s experience and lessons could translate to different contexts across Europe and Central Asia.




About the session




Date & time:

 

15 October, 16:00 – 17:30 CEST

Location:

 Online via Zoom

Cost:

 Free

Target audience:

 Trans communities and activists 










Register here










What the session will cover 




Trans Healthcare Actions will share how Kindred was created through co-creation between the local trans community and allied healthcare professionals, and walk us through the clinic’s foundation, model, structure, services and vision.




The session will also explore how the Irish social, legal and medical landscape shaped their approach, and invite participants to think about their own contexts: What gaps exist in trans healthcare? What community networks and resources are already available? What might help or hinder efforts to build similar community-led care?

author: TGEU
title: TGEU contributes expertise to new guidance on SOGIE rights in detention
content:
TGEU served on the Expert Advisory Group for the publication Advancing SOGIE Rights in Detention: Promising Practices, a new guidance note published by the 

Association for the Prevention of Torture

 

(APT). This included providing initial input on the project, reviewing a first draft during a consultation meeting in Geneva in March 2026, and providing expert feedback on an advanced draft.




The publication documents promising practices by governments, prison administrations, staff and oversight bodies to improve conditions for LGBTI people in detention. It pays particular attention to trans communities and highlights approaches that address the structural challenges faced by LGBTI people deprived of liberty.




The publication was presented during a dedicated session at the TGEU Trans Council in Ljubljana on 11 September 2026.










read the publication










Advancing SOGIE Rights in Detention: Promising Practices is available in English, Spanish, French and Portuguese.




Your support makes change possible
